basics.name: Avner Bensoussan
basics.label: PhD Candidate in Computer Science
basics.summary: PhD candidate in Computer Science working on quantum software testing and verification, with a focus on faults in Hybrid Quantum–Classical architectures and information-theoretic approaches to software testability.

work.name: King's College London
work.summary: PhD research on testing and verification of Hybrid Quantum–Classical software architectures. Member of King’s Quantum and the Software Systems (SSY) research group, contributing to the RoarQ (Robust and Reliable Quantum Computing) collaboration and the VSL-Q project.
highlights: Defined the Quantum Squeeziness information-theoretic testability metric
Developed the first taxonomy of real faults in Hybrid Quantum–Classical architectures published in ACM TOSEM
Co-supervised 5 BSc thesis projects at King’s College London, in industrial collaboration with Applied Quantum Computing, based on OOPSLA 2025 publication AccelerQ
PC Member for IEEE Quantum Week 2026

work.name: King's College London
work.summary: Research on testing approaches for autonomous vehicles using Carla and ROS.
highlights: Designed experiments to evaluate realism in simulation environments

courses: Final Project: Testing the Ethical Decision-Making of Autonomous Vehicles

publications.name: Quantum Squeeziness: An Information Theoretical Metric for Quantum Software Testability
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
publications.summary: Defines the fundations of Quantum Software testability and introduces Quantum Squeeziness, an information-theoretic metric for evaluating quantum software testability and fault detectability. The approach quantifies fault masking and demonstrates its relationship with mutation testing effectiveness across more than 50,000 mutants.

publications.name: Toward Live Noise Fingerprinting for Discrepancy Analysis in Quantum Software Engineering
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the 19th IEEE International Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST 2026)
publications.summary: Presents SIMSHADOW, a classical shadow tomography-based approach for live fingerprinting of quantum hardware noise. It uses noise fingerprints to identify discrepancies across quantum platforms, supporting more effective testing, debugging, and validation of quantum software.

publications.name: A Taxonomy of Real Faults in Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures
publications.publisher: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
publications.summary: Develops an empirical taxonomy of real faults in hybrid quantum-classical architectures based on more than 5,000 GitHub issues. Identifies and classifies 133 real faults, providing insights into fault characteristics and opportunities for improving debugging and quality assurance.

publications.name: AccelerQ: Accelerating Quantum Eigensolver Algorithms With Machine Learning
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA 2025)
publications.summary: Introduces AccelerQ, a machine-learning-based framework for optimising quantum eigensolver algorithms. It combines genetic algorithms and machine learning models to automatically tune quantum program parameters, improving computational accuracy and efficiency.

publications.name: Shaking Up Quantum Simulators with Fuzzing and Rigour
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA 2025)
publications.summary: Introduces FuzzQ, a rigorous fuzzing framework for detecting bugs in quantum simulators through formal modelling, differential testing, mutation testing, and invariant checking. Its evaluation identifies eight simulator bugs, including six previously undocumented bugs.

publications.name: Synthetic versus Real: An Analysis of Critical Scenarios for Autonomous Vehicle Testing
publications.summary: Presents a quantitative methodology for evaluating the realism of synthetic critical scenarios used in autonomous vehicle testing. It compares simulated collision scenarios against real-world crash data to assess realism and improve scenario generation.

publications.name: Exploring LLM-Driven Explanations for Quantum Algorithms
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2024)
publications.summary: Investigates the use of large language models to automatically explain quantum algorithms and improve developer understanding of quantum software. Evaluates multiple language models across seven quantum algorithms, examining explanation quality, consistency, and the effects of contextual prompting.

publications.name: Fuzzing-Based Differential Testing for Quantum Simulators
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the 16th International Symposium on Search-Based Software Engineering (SSBSE 2024), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
publications.summary: Proposes a grammar-based fuzzing and differential testing approach for detecting inconsistencies in quantum simulators. Generates valid quantum programs and compares their execution across multiple platforms to identify simulator bugs, crashes, hangs, and behavioural discrepancies.

projects.name: A Taxonomy of Real Faults in Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures
projects.summary: Published taxonomy of real-world faults in Hybrid Quantum–Classical software architectures.

projects.name: King’s Quantum
projects.summary: King’s Quantum is a multidisciplinary research initiative across King’s College London, integrating expertise from physics, computer science, engineering, and life sciences departments. It develops transformative quantum technologies for healthcare, life sciences, security, and industry, promoting collaboration between academic departments and industry partners to apply quantum computing, sensing, and simulation in real-world challenges.

projects.name: RoaRQ
projects.summary: RoaRQ is a UK-wide inter-university collaboration, led by Oxford University, and includes researchers from King's College London and 11 other world-class UK universities. It focuses on developing robust, fault-tolerant quantum computing systems and reliable quantum software, emphasizing cross-university collaboration in quantum fault analysis, verification, and error mitigation.

projects.name: VSL-Q (Verified Simulation for Large Quantum Systems)
projects.summary: VSL-Q develops verified simulation techniques for large-scale quantum systems, combining quantum simulation methods with formal verification to ensure correctness and reliability of simulations.
